extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalists, and public-relations practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or designing press releases for media pickup based on the negotiated-control framework: how a source's control over information and its ongoing relationship with journalists determine likelihood and quality of pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources control information; journalists control publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources control information; journalists control publication. Each side has resources the other needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat press releases as moves in a negotiation where each party brings leverage: sources provide access to information, journalists provide access to audience. Releases should be designed with that reciprocal dependence in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access is negotiated continuously
rubrics_metrics.description: Access is negotiated continuously, not granted once. Each release is an episode in a longer dance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate releases in context of an ongoing relationship: short-term gains (e.g., strict control) can damage future access; consistent reliability earns pickup over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control–access trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources differ on a control–access trade-off: more control over the message means less media access; more access means less control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design releases by choosing an appropriate point on the control–access continuum according to the issuer's strategic posture; avoid extremes that undermine desired outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different sources favor different control-access settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: Different sources favor different control–access settlements: police and courts seek high control; advocacy groups accept lower control for higher access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match release formality, constraints (embargoes, review rights), and openness to the typical expectations of your source type and the beat's norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control-access trade-off discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: A release that demands too much control (right to review, no-quote conditions, embargoed-only release) will be picked up less. A release that surrenders all control (open data dump) will be picked up but framed by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid demanding excessive formal controls; similarly, avoid giving away all framing power. Choose the trade-off appropriate to the issuer's strategic posture and long-term relationship goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiation continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Each release is part of an ongoing relationship. Burn the relationship by misleading the journalist on this release, lose pickup on the next twenty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistency and honesty across releases. Consider how a single release affects future willingness of journalists to cover you; avoid tactics that erode trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information-asymmetry leverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources can supply context only they have; releases that leverage this asymmetric advantage (insider expertise, on-the-ground witnesses) earn deeper pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include unique access, exclusive data, eyewitness accounts, or expert availability that reporters cannot easily obtain elsewhere to increase the chance of substantive coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat-source access bargain
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources who reliably supply the beat's news in exchange for cooperative coverage maintain pickup; sources who provide only press releases without follow-up access lose ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a pattern of useful, timely contribution to a beat (timely tips, interviews, background) rather than relying solely on one-off releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk-of-attribution awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources should consider what attribution risks the journalist faces; on-record release with named spokesperson reduces journalist risk and increases pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear on-the-record spokespeople and attribution-friendly materials to lower reporters' barriers to using your information; be aware that anonymous or unattributed claims reduce pickup likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendability under scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Each release should withstand a journalist's editor asking "is this defensible?" — releases that pass this defendability check are run; releases that don't trigger callbacks or rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate editorial vetting: provide verifiable facts, sources, documentation, and plausible claims so editors can defend running the story if questioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-tier release architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Some releases are designed for control (carefully crafted, embargoed); others for access (background packets, expert availability). A sophisticated release program operates both tiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure communications into controlled, high-precision releases when necessary and looser, access-oriented materials to cultivate pickup and relationships; use each tier for its strategic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-journalist bargain renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: When the issuer's access bargain has degraded (after a missed embargo, an inaccurate release), releases should explicitly acknowledge this and offer a corrective action to rebuild trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If trust is damaged, use releases or direct outreach to apologize, correct errors, explain remedies, and offer compensatory access or material to restore the relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative-cooperation supply
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources who supply investigative material (FOI documents, internal reviews) build access credit even when individual releases fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contribute substantive documents or leads that help investigative reporting to accrue long-term goodwill and access, which can translate into pickup beyond routine releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police/court/regulator-style precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases from heavily-routinized sources (police, courts, regulators) get auto-pickup because the negotiation is institutionalized; a release from a non-routinized source must rebuild the negotiation each time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the advantage of institutional routinization: if you lack it, compensate by building reliable patterns of access and defendability to reduce friction for journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickup-worthiness as negotiation quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Pickup-worthiness is dominantly a function of the quality of the source-journalist negotiation the release sits within, not just text quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimize releases for long-term relationship management (appropriate control-access trade-offs, reliability, unique information, and trust repair) rather than only short-term message control; respecting the negotiation sustains pickup over time.
